reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Refers to gas within the bowel wall, which is a radiological sign rather than a single disease and spans a spectrum from entirely benign to life-threatening
The central task is to separate benign (primary or idiopathic) pneumatosis from that caused by bowel ischaemia or necrosis, where it is an ominous finding

Benign forms may be idiopathic (pneumatosis cystoides) or associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, connective tissue disease, or certain drugs and are often asymptomatic incidental findings
Alarming features include abdominal pain out of proportion to signs, peritonism, lactic acidosis, and gas in the portal or mesenteric venous system
Cross-sectional imaging is central to assessment, correlating the pattern of intramural gas with the clinical picture
Benign, asymptomatic pneumatosis is generally managed conservatively, whereas suspected ischaemia or necrosis requires urgent surgical evaluation
Portomesenteric venous gas in an unwell patient greatly raises concern for transmural ischaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Pneumatosis intestinalis denotes the presence of gas within the wall of the bowel, and several mechanisms are proposed. In the benign cystic form, gas is thought to track into the submucosa and subserosa either mechanically (for example through mucosal breaks, raised intraluminal pressure, or from the lungs via the mediastinum in chronic lung disease) or through the action of gas-forming luminal bacteria. In the sinister form, ischaemia disrupts the mucosal barrier and, combined with bacterial gas production and gas dissection into damaged wall and mesenteric veins, signals transmural injury and impending or established necrosis; the same radiological sign therefore reflects widely differing underlying processes.
additionalDifferentials: Iatrogenic causes such as recent endoscopy or surgery
Emphysematous gastritis or infection with gas-forming organisms
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography to define the distribution of intramural gas, assess bowel wall enhancement, and detect portomesenteric venous gas
Serum lactate and arterial blood gas to detect metabolic acidosis suggesting ischaemia
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Plain abdominal and erect chest radiography to identify free air or the intramural gas pattern
Assessment for associated conditions such as chronic lung disease, connective tissue disease, or relevant drug therapy
Endoscopy in selected stable cases to characterise mucosal or cystic lesions
redFlags: Abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings suggesting mesenteric ischaemia
Portal or mesenteric venous gas on imaging in an unwell patient
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause: benign, idiopathic pneumatosis is often self-limiting or stable with an excellent outlook, whereas pneumatosis due to bowel ischaemia or necrosis, particularly with portomesenteric venous gas, carries a high mortality without prompt surgical intervention.
pitfalls: Reflexively operating on benign incidental pneumatosis or, conversely, observing ischaemic pneumatosis that needs urgent surgery
Relying on the radiological sign alone without integrating the clinical picture and lactate
Underestimating the significance of portomesenteric venous gas in an unwell patient
Overlooking a drug or lung-disease association that explains a benign form
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Determine the underlying cause first, as management diverges sharply between benign and ischaemic pneumatosis
Urgent surgical evaluation and laparotomy with resection of non-viable bowel for suspected ischaemia or necrosis, especially with peritonism, lactic acidosis or portomesenteric venous gas
Bowel rest, intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics with close observation in equivocal or unwell patients
Conservative management for benign, asymptomatic pneumatosis cystoides, sometimes with high-concentration oxygen therapy to promote resorption of intramural gas
Identify and treat associated conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or connective tissue disease, and review culprit drugs
Serial clinical, biochemical (lactate, inflammatory markers) and imaging monitoring if deterioration occurs
Escalate to surgical and critical care teams when features of transmural injury emerge
